title: Token slicing and seam effects eval
content:
Summary:
This note documents an exploratory eval for how token-level slicing (where requests are split into segments for retrieval+generation) creates seam effects that reduce recall and trigger attention-sink conditions across long contexts (8k, 32k, 128k). Goal is to create a compact reproducible probe + prompt set, capture metrics that matter for onboarding a candidate model variant, and propose mitigation experiments (kv-cache stitching, seam-aware attention masks, retrieval-window overlap).

Motivation / hypotheses:
- Hypothesis A: When input is split into contiguous shards for retrieval+generation, the model's attention patterns will underweight tokens near shard boundaries, reducing recall of entities introduced just before the seam ("seam fade").
- Hypothesis B: Certain prompt styles (multi-turn with system/meta tokens repeated) amplify KV-cache fragmentation and lead to an effective "attention sink" where the model over-focuses on the last N tokens, making earlier long-span retrieval signals vanish.
- Hypothesis C: Overlapping retrieval windows (small overlap, e.g., 64–256 tokens) mitigate seam fade but increase compute; a stitching algorithm that merges KV-cache entries with attention correction can approach the overlap baseline with lower cost.

Test matrix (high-level):
- Models: candidate-v1 (baseline), candidate-v1-quant (int8), candidate-v2 (revised attention bias)
- Context lengths: 8k, 32k, 128k
- Retrieval behavior: contiguous shards (no overlap), shards with 128-token overlap, single large retrieval (when feasible)
- Prompt styles: single-document summarization, multi-document Q&A chain (explicit doc separators), conversational chat with system prefix repeated every 512 tokens (simulates tool calls inserted)
- Metrics captured per run: exact-match recall on probe entities, token-level attention mass heatmap summary (start/middle/end thirds), KV-cache hit/miss rate, latency P50/P90, token cost estimate

Infrastructure / how we ran it:
- Serving: dedicated test cluster (4x A100-80GB), runtime v1.12 with KV-cache tracing enabled
- Retriever: FAISS index sharded by document, retrieval window size variable per experiment
- Harness: local harness that records per-token attention aggregates and snapshots KV-cache keys at seam points
- Runs: 100 probes per configuration (randomized doc ordering), deterministic seeds recorded in linked_artifacts

Probe construction and prompt set (representative examples):
1) Entity recall probe (single-shot):
PROMPT: "You are an assistant. Return the exact year when <ENTITY> first appeared in the document. If not present, say NOT_FOUND."
Context: long document with entity mention placed either 32 tokens before seam, 4 tokens before seam, 64 tokens after seam. We vary position to measure seam fade.

2) Multi-doc chain (chain-of-thought disabled):
PROMPT: "Given the documents below, find all products mentioned and list them sorted by first mention. Use ONLY the text in the documents."
Documents: 12 short docs concatenated to reach target context size. Separator token = <DOC_END>. We vary whether retriever shards split between doc boundaries or inside a doc to exercise seam within-doc vs inter-doc.

3) Conversational with repeated system prefix:
PROMPT: System prefix repeated every 512 tokens: "SYSTEM: keep answers concise; prefer numeric dates". User turn asks for a timeline referencing multiple retrieved paragraphs across the context. This tests repeated instruction tokens creating KV-cache duplicates and sink patterns.

Observed results (condensed):
- Seam fade (contiguous shards, no overlap): entity recall drop of ~14% at 8k, ~21% at 32k, and ~34% at 128k when entity sits 4 tokens before seam versus 32 tokens before seam. Fallback to NOT_FOUND increased proportionally.
- Overlap baseline (128-token overlap): reduced recall drop to 3–7% across lengths but incurred ~8–12% extra token cost on average.
- KV-cache tracing shows majority of misses correspond to cache entries created at the end of a shard that were not consulted after a subsequent shard's warmup tokens were processed (evidence of fragmentation).
- Attention mass summary: models show a strong tail-slope where last 512 tokens hold 42–58% attention mass in worst cases (higher for candidate-v1-quant), indicating attention sink behavior. candidate-v2 reduces last-512 mass by ~9 percentage points on average.
- Prompt style sensitivity: the repeated system prefix amplifies sink: recall drops a further 6–10% vs the same prompt without repeated prefix.

Sample numeric table (text):
Config | Context | Seam pos | Recall drop vs in-shard baseline
contiguous | 8k | 4 tokens before seam | 14%
contiguous | 32k | 4 tokens before seam | 21%
contiguous | 128k | 4 tokens before seam | 34%
overlap128 | 128k | 4 tokens before seam | 5%

Regression flags for onboarding checklist (candidate-v1 -> candidate-v2 comparison):
- Regression 1 (acceptance): If recall at seam position (4 tokens) decreases by >10% relative to baseline model, fail onboarding. candidate-v1-quant failed at 32k and 128k under contiguous shards.
- Perf guardrail: latency P90 should not exceed baseline by >15% for comparable recall; overlap solution violates this in our cluster tests.

Root-cause hypothesis from traces:
- The runtime constructs per-shard KV maps keyed by local token offsets; when shards are stitched, key collisions and reindexing produce stale references. The model's attention cache lookup routine retrieves more recent shard entries preferentially, starving the earlier seam tokens so their contribution to attention is effectively masked.
- Quantization appears to exacerbate this via compressed KV embeddings being less robust to noisy re-alignment, explaining candidate-v1-quant worse performance.

Quick diagnostics we used (repro steps):
1) Create short synthetic doc with entity at N tokens from seam. 2) Serve with trace flags: KV_DUMP=true, ATT_HEATMAP=true. 3) Compare attention mass including and excluding KV entries that originated before the seam. 4) Run with overlap 0/64/128 to see recall slope.

Mitigations explored (short):
- Stitched KV merging: patch runtime to merge KV entries across shards using global offsets (experiment PR linked). This recovered ~60–80% of seam fade for candidate-v1 with negligible latency increase in the test cluster.
- Seam-aware attention bias: apply a small learned bias that increases attention weight for tokens within 128 tokens before shard end; candidate-v2 integrates an attention-bias layer and shows consistent improvement with lower compute than overlap approach.
- Retriever-side overlap heuristic: use 128-token overlap only when entity-detection confidence is low (binary classifier), reducing average cost. Effective but adds complexity in retriever pipeline.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How do these seam effects interact with function/tool-calls and structured output? We observed malformed JSON more frequently when seam occurs inside an argument list. Need a separate probe.
- Long-term: should we enforce global offsets encoding in KV keys across all runtimes to avoid fragmentation-forced regressions?
- Does dynamic batching (requests with different slice boundaries sharing a GPU) amplify fragmentation? Early traces suggest yes; schedule a SRE test with mixed-slice batches.

Next steps / action items (owners):
- Miguel: finish PR for KV-stitching (GH #4678) and add regression test harness for seam positions (due 2025-02-01).
- Lina: run expanded A/B across candidate-v2 over 3 cloud regions and report latency/recall tradeoffs (due 2025-02-10).
- Evan: add structured-output seam probe (function-call JSON bracket test) and run 1k trials at 32k (due 2025-01-30).
- Aisha: write onboarding acceptance criteria doc that includes seam recall guardrails and add to candidate onboards checklist (due 2025-02-07).

Notes to self (rough):
- Keep the synthetic probes public in the eval repo; the current harness uses synthetic-doc-gen v0.3 (see linked_artifacts).
- Consider telemetry: add a per-request seam-alert metric to Console so teams can find when their live workload hits seaming often.

Appendix: raw example of seam-induced fail (copied from trace):
--- EXAMPLE TRIMMED OUTPUT ---
Context: [DOC1 end ... TOKEN A TOKEN B TOKEN C] | [DOC2 start TOKEN D ...]
Query: "When was TOKEN B introduced?"
Model: "NOT_FOUND"  <-- expected 2017
Trace: KV entries for TOKEN B present at shard_end_kv_ids=[12345], during next shard warmup a remap replaced ids and attention mass for TOKEN B dropped from 0.038 to 0.002
-----------------------------

If accepted as useful, we can fold several of these probes into the standard onboarding suite and mark seam-sensitive behavior as a model-card attribute (e.g., seam_robustness: low/medium/high).

End of note.
